title: Delhi Pollution Irritates Children's Eyes As AQI Hits Very Poor Levels
excerpt: With Delhi's average AQI at 331 on Tuesday, ophthalmologists explain why pollutants trigger redness, itching and watering in children, and which symptoms need prompt care.
body:
• Delhi's average AQI climbed to 331 at 7 a.m. on Tuesday, in the 'very poor' category, with eight stations above 400 in the 'severe' zone, according to CPCB data cited by HealthandMe.
  • Ophthalmologists say dust, smoke, particulate matter and toxic gases can cause redness, itching, burning, excessive watering and dryness in children's eyes.
  • Parents are advised to avoid outdoor activities when pollution is high, keep windows closed during severe pollution, stop eye rubbing and wash children's faces after they come indoors.
  • Seek prompt care for eye pain, significant light sensitivity, blurred or reduced vision, marked redness or difficulty opening the eye.

Ophthalmologists are warning that Delhi's deteriorating air can irritate children's eyes as well as their lungs, triggering redness, itching, burning, excessive watering and dryness.

On Tuesday, the national capital's average Air Quality Index climbed to 331 at 7 a.m., entering the 'very poor' category, according to HealthandMe, citing Central Pollution Control Board data. Eight monitoring stations recorded readings above 400, in the 'severe' zone, and 33 of the city's 58 stations recorded AQI in the 'very poor' category, it said. The India Meteorological Department and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology forecast that air quality is likely to remain in the 'very poor' category over the coming days, according to the same report.

Why children's eyes react

"Children's eyes are more sensitive to irritants in the environment, and exposure to pollutants, particulate matter and toxic gases can irritate the surface of the eye," Dr Shibal Bhartiya, Clinical Director for Ophthalmology at Marengo Asia International Institute of Neuro and Spine, told HealthandMe.

Dr Neepa Thacker Dave, Senior Consultant in Paediatric Ophthalmology at SRCC Children's Hospital, told HealthandMe that the surface of the eye is protected by a delicate tear film that provides lubrication, maintains clear vision and helps defend against environmental irritants. Exposure to airborne pollutants can disturb that layer and contribute to irritation and inflammation, she said.

That helps explain a symptom parents may find confusing. "Excessive watering does not necessarily mean that the eyes are adequately lubricated. Irritation can trigger reflex tearing even when the tear film is unstable. Consequently, children may experience watering alongside dryness or discomfort," Dr Dave said.

Children with existing allergies or sensitive eyes may notice symptoms worsening during periods of high pollution, the experts said, and Dr Bhartiya said long-term exposure to poor air quality may also worsen pre-existing ocular surface conditions.

What parents should do, according to the experts

Reducing exposure is the first step, particularly on days when air quality is poor. Dr Bhartiya advised parents to avoid outdoor activities when pollution levels are high, keep windows closed during periods of severe pollution, encourage children to avoid rubbing their eyes and ensure children wash their faces after coming indoors.

A separate guide from Artemis Hospitals gives similar general advice for smog season: check the AQI daily, limit outdoor exposure and move children's play and exercise indoors on heavily polluted days, and keep windows and doors closed when outdoor pollution is high. Its list of early signs in children includes watery or red eyes alongside cough, wheezing, runny nose and sore throat.

Parents should not simply assume a child will describe what is wrong. Dr Dave said children may not always have the vocabulary to describe eye discomfort, so parents and teachers should watch for frequent eye rubbing, excessive blinking, squinting, watering or reluctance to take part in reading and outdoor activities.

When to see a doctor promptly

Mild irritation may improve when exposure is reduced, but parents should not dismiss eye irritation in children, particularly when pollution levels are high, Dr Dave said. Recurring or persistent symptoms warrant an eye examination, she said.

Some signs require prompt medical attention, according to the HealthandMe report: eye pain, significant sensitivity to light, blurred or reduced vision, marked redness or difficulty opening the eye. Those are the red flags to act on the same day, rather than waiting for the air to clear.

For families in Delhi and for diaspora families with children visiting relatives there, the practical takeaway from the experts is concrete: check the AQI in the morning, keep outdoor play inside when readings are in the very poor or severe range, and treat persistent eye symptoms as a reason for an examination, not as a minor seasonal nuisance.
